n: Abraham’s creation account opens with a council: “Let us go down.” The Gods — plural — organize and form the heavens and earth, shaping existing material rather than creating from nothing.
Once formed, the earth is empty and dark, covered by deep water, while the Spirit of the Gods broods over it like a bird warming its nest — life is about to come.

f.g: Compare Genesis 1:2, “without form, and void” (Hebrew tohu wa-bohu).
hovering protectively, as a bird over its eggs; a fitting sense of the Hebrew merahefet.

n: The Gods command light into existence, and light appears. Light is the first gift of creation.
The Gods “comprehended” the light — they understood it fully — and divided it from the darkness. Compare Genesis, where God “saw” the light was good.
The Gods name light Day and darkness Night, establishing the first cycle of night and day. Abraham speaks of creative “times” rather than strict 24-hour days.
The Gods plan an “expanse” to separate waters above from waters below. Abraham’s “expanse” clarifies the KJV word “firmament.”

f.g: Hebrew raqia‘, a spread-out sky; the KJV translates it “firmament.”

n: The Gods “ordered” the expanse, and it was done exactly as commanded. A recurring theme in Abraham: creation obeys its Creators.
The expanse is named Heaven (the sky), closing the second creative time.

f.g: Here, the visible sky or atmosphere.

n: The Gods order the waters to gather in one place so dry land can appear, and it happens as ordered.

f.w: let the earth come up dry

n: The dry land is named Earth and the gathered waters Great Waters. The Gods see that they were obeyed — Abraham emphasizes obedience where Genesis says “it was good.”

f.w: the Gods saw that they were obeyed
f.g: Genesis 1:10 reads “God saw that it was good.”

n: The Gods prepare the earth to bring forth grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees, each reproducing its own kind.

f.g: according to its own kind or species.

n: The earth is organized so each plant comes from its own seed and can only reproduce its own kind — a stable, orderly pattern of life.

f.w: whose seed could only bring forth the same in itself

n: The Gods “numbered the days,” completing the third time. The word “time” suggests creative periods of undetermined length.

f.g: Abraham uses “time” where Genesis has “day,” leaving the duration open.

n: The Gods organize lights in the sky to separate day and night and to mark signs, seasons, days, and years — giving humanity a calendar and a way to read time.
These lights are to shine upon the earth, and it is done.

f.w: to give light upon the earth

n: The two great lights — sun and moon — are organized to rule day and night, along with the stars. Chapter 3 gave Abraham a deeper view of these same bodies.
The Gods place these lights in the heavens to illuminate the earth and divide light from darkness.

f.w: to rule over the day and over the night

n: A verse found only in Abraham: the Gods watched what they had commanded “until they obeyed.” Creation is pictured as patient, purposeful work over time.

f.g: kept watch over; implies patient attention through a process.

n: Night and day mark the close of the fourth time.
The Gods plan for the waters to teem with living creatures and for birds to fly across the open sky.

f.g: Abraham often speaks of preparing or planning, suggesting this chapter describes the plan before the physical creation of chapter 5.

n: The waters are prepared for great sea creatures, swimming life, and birds of every kind. The Gods see that their plan is good and will be obeyed.

f.g: Hebrew tanninim — great sea creatures in general.

n: The Gods plan to bless these creatures to multiply and fill the seas and earth. Fruitfulness is a blessing from God.
Night and day mark the fifth time.
The earth is prepared to bring forth land creatures: cattle, creeping things, and wild beasts, each after its kind.

f.g: small animals that move close to the ground — insects, reptiles, and the like.

n: The earth is organized to bring forth every kind of land animal, and the Gods foresee that it will obey.

f.w: the Gods saw they would obey

n: The crowning act: the Gods counsel together and plan to form man in their own image and likeness, giving humanity stewardship over all creatures.

f.w: in our image, after our likeness

f.g: rule as a steward, with responsibility for what is entrusted.

n: The Gods go down to organize mankind in their own image, male and female. Both men and women bear the divine image.
The Gods bless man and woman: to have children, fill the earth, subdue it, and care for its creatures.

f.g: to bring under control and make productive.

n: Seed-bearing plants and fruit are given to humans as food. “Meat” here simply means food.

f.g: food in general, not just animal flesh.

n: Animals, birds, and creeping things are also given life and green plants for food. Every creature has its provision in God’s plan.
The Gods resolve to carry out all they have planned and foresee that creation will be “very obedient.” The sixth time ends with the whole plan in place.
